extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, policymakers, and practitioners interested in information policy, law, technology, and the political economy of the Internet
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly book-chapter–level exposition that defines, analyzes, and evaluates the emergence, characteristics, and political-legal implications of the 'networked information economy' and its effects on autonomy, democracy, culture, and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Networked information economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A new stage in the information economy characterized by decentralized individual action, important cooperative and coordinated action carried out through radically distributed, nonmarket mechanisms that do not depend on proprietary strategies; catalyzed by declining costs of computation, communication, and storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that this replaces the industrial information economy and is enabled by the fabrication technology of computation and pervasive networks; look for indicators such as distributed material means of production and large-scale decentralized coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralization and distribution of production means
rubrics_metrics.description: The material requirements for effective information production—computers, networks, storage—are distributed to many more individuals than before, enabling individuals or small groups to produce and communicate widely without large centralized physical capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of low-cost access to processors, networks, and storage among broad populations; consider reach (e.g., 'on the order of a billion people').

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of nonproprietary and nonmarket strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonmarket and nonproprietary motivations and organizational forms (education, arts, sciences, political debate) are inherently important in information production and become more significant as physical barriers fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent to which projects depend on openness, sharing norms, and nonexclusive licensing versus proprietary exclusion; examples include free software and open educational resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rise of nonmarket individual production and coordinate effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual action, even when uncoordinated, can produce aggregate coordinate effects that supply rich information goods (illustrated by the example of Google search results produced by many diverse actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the degree to which outputs emerge from many loosely motivated actors rather than centralized editorial/market actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer production and large-scale cooperative efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective, large-scale cooperative efforts (peer production) can produce high-quality information and software—examples include GNU/Linux, Wikipedia, and SETI@Home—challenging conventional firm-based production models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify volunteer-based, distributed projects that sustain complex cooperative outputs without traditional hierarchical market firms; consider scale, voluntary contribution, and quality outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced individual autonomy as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The networked information economy improves individuals' practical capacities in three ways: (1) doing more for themselves independently, (2) doing more in loose commonality with others without pricing/hierarchy, and (3) doing more within formal organizations outside markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess projects or environments by how they expand these three dimensions of autonomy—e.g., enabling self-publishing, loose collaboration, or nonmarket organizational participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networked public sphere vs mass-mediated public sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A shift from mass-mediated public sphere to a networked public sphere that enables many more individuals to communicate and participate in public discourse, potentially remedying mass media failures (limited intake basin, concentrated power, programming toward the inane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a communication environment widens participation, reduces gatekeeping by concentrated media owners, and supports substantive political discourse rather than superficial programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing the Babel objection and information overload
rubrics_metrics.description: The networked public sphere must respond to critiques that 'when everyone can speak, no one can be heard' (Babel objection) and to concerns about concentration of attention; mechanisms like mailing lists, writable web capabilities, mobility, and social systems for collection/accreditation ameliorate overload without recreating mass-media gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for decentralized filtering, social accreditation, and affordances that surface politically salient information without transferring filtering power to wealthy gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of production strategies as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Information production uses a diversity of strategies (market, nonmarket, proprietary, commons-based); understanding this diversity is crucial to evaluating sustainability and normative claims about the networked environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which mix of strategies is present, the incentives supporting them, and the contexts in which nonmarket strategies can be as or more efficient than market ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a commons-based infrastructural ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: For social production to flourish, a core common infrastructure—open physical, logical, and content-layer resources—is required so that users can create, encode, render, and receive new statements freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess availability/openness of infrastructure (open wireless, open standards, device platforms, freely available content) and legal protections or constraints affecting such openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and institutional constraints that favor enclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent legal trends (longer/more expansive copyrights, stronger trademarks, expanded patents, anticircumvention rules like DMCA) skew the institutional ecology toward proprietary models and create barriers to nonmarket production and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating policy or institutional design, account for how changes in IP law, regulatory rules, and enforcement affect the feasibility of commons-based models and social production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countervailing social and technological trends toward openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Social movements and technological practices (free software, Creative Commons, Open Access, NIH guidelines, open archiving) create countervailing pressures by producing large quantities of freely reusable information and by reshaping business models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify social movements, open-licensing practices, and industry shifts that expand commons-based content and evaluate their scale and sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology as enabling but not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological conditions (fabrication tech, networks) make certain arrangements feasible, but institutional choices, law, and social practices determine how those technologies shape markets, freedom, and distribution of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid technological determinism; evaluate policy, firm behavior, and social movements that mediate technological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs and political stakes: redistribution of wealth and power
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of social production promises redistribution of wealth and power away from incumbent firms toward individuals, social groups, and new business models, creating political battles with high normative stakes for autonomy, democracy, culture, and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising policy proposals or institutional changes, consider distributive impacts and the political economy of incumbents vs emergent actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on justice and global human development
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonmarket, nonexclusive production can reduce access barriers and contribute to human development—education, health, innovation—by making information and tools more widely available, particularly for low- and middle-income countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate initiatives by their capacity to lower costs of access to knowledge and innovation tools, and consider evidence from sectors like free software, open standards, and open educational resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding and case-based validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about the networked information economy should be grounded in technical, economic, and social evidence (case studies of software, encyclopedias, reporting, entertainment) because they run counter to standard industrial-economy intuitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor analyses that include detailed case studies and rigorous economic reasoning when assessing whether nonmarket production is sustainable and effective.
